newsitem.title: UK: Brown defends UK budget as stocks stage rally.
newsitem.headline: Brown defends UK budget as stocks stage rally.

text.p: British shares surged to all-time highs on Thursday as the London stockmarket gave finance minister Gordon Brown the benefit of the doubt over the Labour Party's first budget in 18 years.

Brown basked in praise from newspapers for Wednesday's "budget for the people" designed to fulfil Labour's election pledges to get the unemployed back to work and lay the foundations of steady growth over the long term.

An opinion poll showed that ordinary Britons thought he had done a good job. Shares began sharply lower as traders focussed on the view that Brown had not done enough to curb the booming economy, raising the prospect of an interest rate rise next week to cool consumer demand.

But the early losses dissolved as the view took hold that the budget held no major shocks for industry, although Brown hit utilities with a stinging windfall tax, and would not halt the forward march of Britain's buoyant economy.
The key FTSE-100 index of leading shares was 52.3 points up at 4,803.7 by mid-morning, eclipsing a previous high of 4,796 seen on June 13.
Sterling was firm on expectation of higher interest rates, reaching new five-year highs against the mark at 2.9427 and nearing $1.6785, before slipping back slightly.
Brown filled out more of the details of his budget on Thursday, revealing he plans tougher than expected cuts in benefits for unemployed people who refuse to work or train.
He said he wanted a stable, competitive pound and that "nobody can be happy" about an 18 percent rise in its value, which is causing severe pain to exporters. He gave no timescale for the rise.

A key move in Brown's budget -- which set a five-year plan to cut the budget deficit and eased key corporate taxes -- was a cut in tax credits for institutional investors like pension funds on dividend payouts.
The Conservatives, routed in Labour's May 1 election landslide, said this was a move which would hit every pensioner in the land.
The main opposition party said individuals would have to make higher pension contributions and local authorities would have to increase local taxes to make up pension shortfalls.
But Brown dismissed the warnings. "There is no question that in the long term and the medium term it will be good for companies and it will be good for pensioners.

"I really have very little time for those who are critical of the changes that we have made. When they sit down and think about it, they will realise they will benefit pensioners as well as the country as a whole."
The first opinion poll on the budget in London's Evening Standard newspaper showed a clear majority believed Brown had done a good job.

Only eight percent of those questioned in the NOP poll felt they would be better off, compared to 47 percent who felt they would suffer. But a majority -- 53 percent -- blamed the ousted Conservatives for the pain. Less than a fifth blamed Brown.
And overall 54 percent thought Brown did a good job, compared to just 13 percent who were critical.

Newspapers praised Brown's decision to raid the government's emergency reserves to provide 3.5 billion pounds ($5.9 billion) for hospitals and schools, a move that went down well with left-wingers in the Labour party.
Brown also announced a 4.8 billion pound one-off excess profits tax on utility companies to fund a "welfare to work" scheme to help jobless youths and single parents.

The moves meant that Brown was able to apply a modest brake on Britain's booming economy, which experts had seen as essential to ward off inflationary pressures, without a major immediate effect on the consumers who voted Labour into office.

But financial analysts were convinced that the Bank of England would decide to raise interest rates by at least 0.25 percentage point next week from 6.50 percent. Official rates have been increased twice since Labour won the election.
($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
